39: Barbecue is one of the easiest things for a client to search for and one of the hardest to deliver well at an event. According to DataForSEO (October 2026), people in the U.S. search "bbq catering" about 9,900 times a month and "bbq catering near me" about 18,100 times. Those are buyers, not future owners: the person who wants to start the business searches "bbq business plan" about 70 times a month. Demand comes from companies ordering lunches, families planning graduations and birthdays, and couples booking weddings. This plan is for a pitmaster who wants to serve all three without running a restaurant. We smoke in a permitted commissary, serve or deliver at the client's venue, and keep the smoker trailer for the events that pay for it.
40: The concept is a full-service, off-site BBQ caterer. The pitmaster smokes brisket, pulled pork, ribs, chicken and sausage in the commissary yard, holds it hot in insulated food carriers and hot boxes, and serves it from a staffed buffet with a carving station. The smoker trailer goes to the event only for weddings and premium bookings, as a paid add-on we call a live pit on site. The owner's pickup is the tow vehicle, so it carries no cost in the plan. Drop-off lunches for companies are the second line, and live-fire menus (Argentine asado, Santa Maria tri-tip, whole hog in a La Caja China) are the premium line. What we keep from the open-fire tradition is the show: cooking to the probe and carving in front of the guests, because that moment is part of what the client pays for.
41: The total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} in startup costs plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The heaviest lines are the smoker trailer ({{inv_vehiculo}}), the used cargo van ({{inv_furgoneta}}), the holding and service equipment ({{inv_holding}}), the launch budget ({{inv_lanzamiento}}) and the live-fire rig ({{inv_rig}}). We do not build or lease a restaurant, which keeps the investment well below a venue with its own dining room and kitchen. We cover it with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. A loan of that size does not fit the $50,000 SBA Microloan cap, so the realistic routes are a bank loan or an SBA 7(a) loan, and no plan can promise a lender's answer.
42: In year 1 we plan {{eventos_a1}} events with an average of {{invitados_evento}} guests at {{precio_invitado}} per guest, excluding sales tax. That adds up to {{ventas_a1}} in revenue, growing to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3 as events rise to {{eventos_a2}} and {{eventos_a3}}. Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales, the lowest debt service coverage is {{dscr_min}}, and the business breaks even at {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year. Be honest about what this case is: a full-time owner with a pit cook and a $10,000 marketing budget, not the average first year. A new operator more often lands near $300,000 in sales in year 1, so read these numbers as a well-run target and change the inputs to your own.
43: The founding team is small. The owner is the pitmaster, who also sells and buys. A pit cook or lead cook runs the second shift at the smoker, event staff (servers, buffet attendants and carvers) work event by event, and a prep cook doubles as the van driver. Everyone except the owner is a part-time hourly W-2 employee. That makes {{plantilla_puestos}} people, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents. Replace this paragraph with your own background: a lender wants to see who has run a pit and who has sold events. The plan shows that a BBQ caterer can start without a restaurant and with controlled risk, as long as every event is quoted, deposited and staffed on purpose.
46: Our clients buy an event that goes well, not just meat. Companies, usually through an office manager or a planner, want smoked BBQ that arrives hot and on time, as boxed lunches, drop-off trays or a staffed buffet, with an invoice that fits company rules. Families book graduations, birthdays and anniversaries and want one person to handle the menu, the timeline and the cleanup. Couples book weddings months ahead and want the pit, the carving and the tasting to feel personal. A smaller group of premium clients pays for live fire. All of them want safe food at the right temperature, no logistics to think about and a quote with no surprises. The sales cycle differs: companies reorder, while couples book once.
47: Our value proposition rests on three pillars. First, real smoke and real fire: brisket and pork butt cooked low and slow over post oak or hickory, with a proper bark and smoke ring, and a pitmaster who carves at the station and explains the meat. That moment is sold as an experience, not just a plate. Second, regional menu styles the client can pick, from Texas to Carolina to Santa Maria, cooked to the probe and held at safe temperatures in insulated carriers until service. Third, reliability: allergens written into every quote, a tasting before the contract, arrival with time to spare and a propane backup when a burn ban rules out solid fuel. Each pillar gives us a reason to compete on the experience and stay out of the price war over the cheapest tray.
48: We quote by the guest, excluding sales tax and with staffing and the service charge included, and the average is {{precio_invitado}}. With {{invitados_evento}} guests per event, the average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}. BBQ packages are {{cuota_paquetes_pct}} of sales, and the rest are add-ons such as a live pit on site, desserts, rentals and travel fees. A guest minimum protects small events, and a deposit blocks the date: the operators we read, such as Owen's BBQ on Eventective and Hutchins BBQ, ask for 50% nonrefundable. The service charge is part of our price. A voluntary gratuity is not, and it belongs to the staff.
49: We compete against four alternatives. BBQ restaurants that cater on the side have a name, but their pit and crew serve the dining room first. General caterers put barbecue on the menu as one more dish and rarely cook with a pitmaster in front of the guests. Grocery and big-box trays win on price for small orders and lose on service. BBQ food trucks sell a different product, a quick line at a brewery or a lot, so we do not compete with them on speed. We place ourselves in the gap: smoked meat done right, live fire for the events that pay for it, and one person responsible for the event from the quote to the cleanup. We compete on the experience, not on the cheapest tray.
50: Three packages let the client match the event to the budget: drop-off, a full-service BBQ buffet with staff and a carving station, and a live-fire premium menu. A live pit on site is a switch that can be added to any buffet. Ten menu styles give the pitmaster something to sell: Texas, Carolina whole hog, Kansas City burnt ends, Memphis dry-rub ribs, Santa Maria tri-tip over red oak, Argentine asado, Brazilian churrasco, a pig roast in a La Caja China, a fire show with tomahawk steaks and a corporate boxed lunch. Each package has a guest minimum, because small events do not cover the cook and the crew. The pricing calculator builds each quote from your own costs.
53: Demand for BBQ catering comes from the buyer, and search data shows it. According to DataForSEO (October 2026), people in the U.S. search "bbq catering" and "barbecue catering" about 9,900 times a month each and "bbq catering near me" about 18,100 times. Searches for "bbq catering menu" (about 320 a month) and "bbq catering prices" (about 170) have risen over the past six months. These are people who want to hire a caterer, not start one, so they confirm that demand exists without giving us a market size, which we do not quote because every source defines it differently. What matters for you is local: how many venues, offices, campuses and wedding planners sit within an hour of your commissary.
54: Private clients are the most emotional buyers: weddings, rehearsal dinners, graduations and birthdays. They compare photos, reviews and the price per person before they ask for a quote. As a reference, a Texas-style operator in Los Angeles lists $40-$58 per guest for parties and $65-$85 for weddings, with a 30-guest minimum (Eventective, Owen's BBQ). The example prices weddings at $52 per guest, below that Los Angeles range, which is a modest starting point for a sale led by a tasting. Set yours from local quotes. Wedding dates cluster in May and June and again in September and October, so plan your tastings and your cash around them.
55: Corporate clients buy on a different logic. They order boxed BBQ lunches for meetings, drop-off trays for training days, and buffets for openings and holiday parties. The buyer is usually an office manager or a planner who needs a reliable vendor and an invoice that fits company rules. As a reference, Q39 in Kansas City describes drop-off at $15-$30 per person, with its own starting at $17.50, and a staffed buffet for full-service events. Many companies order through corporate catering marketplaces such as ezCater, which the example models at {{marketplace_pct}} of sales with a {{marketplace_comision}} commission. Graduations in May and June, the Fourth of July and holiday parties in December fill the calendar around them.
56: The example mix is a kit estimate, not market data. Of {{eventos_a1}} events, 55 are corporate drop-offs (40 guests at $22), 45 are parties and graduations (70 guests at $35), 22 are full-service company events (110 guests at $36), 20 are weddings (130 guests at $52) and 8 are live-fire premium events (90 guests at $65). Weddings are 13% of the events and 32% of the sales. The calendar is uneven too. The example opens in March, so Month 1 is March, with the peaks in May, June and October and the weakest months in January and February. The lowest cash balance falls in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}} at {{saldo_minimo}}. Rotate the curve to your opening month and replace the shares with what your bookings show.
57: A few trends are worth watching, without leaning on numbers we cannot source. Live fire, such as Argentine asado and Santa Maria tri-tip, gives an event something to watch. Rustic weddings at barn venues and ranches suit a smoker trailer, though the venue decides whether it may cook there. Clients also ask more often for gluten-free, vegetarian and allergy-safe sides, and expect the caterer to handle them without drama.
58: Demand has risks the plan should name. The season is short, so a slow spring can leave a gap that fall may not fill. Clients cancel or cut the guest count late, which is why the deposit and the cancellation terms matter. A burn ban can rule out solid fuel on the day, so the propane backup is not optional. And {{eventos_a1}} events a year is the pace of a full-time operator with a pit cook and a $10,000 marketing budget, not of a typical first year. The pessimistic scenario shows the hit: {{pesimista_eventos}} events and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}, and the cash runs out.
61: Before you set a price, map who competes with you within an hour of your commissary. The list usually includes BBQ restaurants that cater, weekend BBQ caterers, general caterers with a barbecue menu, grocery trays and BBQ food trucks that book private events. For each one, note what the price per guest includes, its guest minimum, whether it cooks on site and what its reviews say. You do not need invented figures: request quotes and read their websites and their reviews on Google and The Knot.
62: Porter's five forces look like this for a BBQ caterer. Supplier power is low to moderate: many meat purveyors, wood and charcoal sellers and equipment dealers compete for your order, although brisket prices swing and a single meatpacker can raise your costs. Buyer power is moderate: clients compare quotes and reviews, but a good tasting and a clear proposal build loyalty, and large corporate accounts push harder on price. The threat of substitutes is real: a BBQ restaurant's catering menu, a grocery tray or a friend with a backyard smoker can replace you on a lower budget. Rivalry peaks in May, June and October, when everyone chases the same Saturdays. The threat of new entrants is moderate: a smoker is easy to buy, but a permitted commissary, insurance that covers the trailer and a fire, a propane backup and the cash for a van take planning, and that slows the hobbyists.
63: Direct competitors are BBQ caterers and BBQ restaurants that serve the same event sizes and the same venues, from weekend operators to full-service companies. Indirect ones are grocery and big-box trays, general caterers with a barbecue menu and the family that rents a smoker for the weekend. To compare fairly, line up the price per guest, what it includes (meats, sides, staff, setup), the guest minimum, whether they cook on site and their reviews on The Knot, WeddingWire, Zola and Google. Then decide where you win: the live pit, the menu styles, the speed of your reply or the clarity of your proposal. Put it in one sentence and use it everywhere.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. You need a permitted commissary kitchen, because there is no legal way to sell food prepared at home, and cottage food rules exclude meat in Texas. If you cook from the trailer at the event, it may count as a mobile food unit with its own permit, so ask your county. Then add the smoker trailer (Yoder Smokers lists offset smokers on trailers from $8,495, and the example budgets {{inv_vehiculo}} for a new 500-gallon class unit), insurance that covers the trailer and a fire, your fire marshal's rules on extinguishers and propane, and the craft of a pitmaster who can repeat a brisket every weekend.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is reliability: arriving with time to spare, with the guest count agreed and the food hot at service. The second is food safety. Cook to the FDA Food Code minimums (145 °F (63 °C) for intact cuts, 155 °F (68 °C) for injected, tenderized or ground meat and sausage, 165 °F (74 °C) for poultry) and hold at 135 °F (57 °C) or above. Those are safety floors, not the finish: brisket is done for quality at about 203 °F (95 °C), when the probe slides in with no resistance. The third is a consistent brisket. The fourth is your relationship with venues and wedding planners, who send many bookings. A small caterer that does all four well can take work from larger rivals.
66: The SWOT for this concept looks like this. Strengths: low fixed costs, since you pay {{ocupacion_anual}} a year for a commissary and trailer parking instead of a restaurant lease, a product people already search for, and a mix of five demand lines. Weaknesses: reliance on a few key people, limited capacity on the busiest Saturdays (the plan allows up to {{capacidad_eventos}} events a year with one trailer and one crew) and an uneven calendar. Opportunities: companies that want a regular vendor, venues and planners with preferred vendor lists, and families who return for the next graduation or birthday. Threats: a foodborne illness, a fire, burn bans, late cancellations, rising meat prices and cheap tray BBQ.
69: The marketing strategy follows two funnels. Weddings and private parties have a long cycle: the client finds you online, asks for a quote, attends a tasting and signs months before the date. Companies have a short, repeating cycle: a well-run lunch leads to the next order and to a referral inside the same office. Graduations and family parties travel by word of mouth. Treat each funnel with its own message and channel, but rest both on the same promise: smoked BBQ that arrives hot and on time, a pitmaster the guests can see and a contract that gives peace of mind.
70: Your website is the main sales tool, because clients read it before they call. It should show the menu styles, "starting at" prices per guest for each type of event, photos of real cooks and a short quote form that asks for the date, the venue, the guest count and allergies. Add an FAQ that answers what people search for: how much barbecue to plan per person, what BBQ catering costs and what happens during a burn ban. Complete your Google Business Profile and keep collecting recent reviews, so you show up when someone searches "bbq catering near me", a phrase with about 18,100 searches a month. Instagram and TikTok videos of the pit and the carving station sell more than any slogan.
71: Directories bring qualified leads when your profile is complete. For weddings, The Knot, WeddingWire and Zola are where couples compare vendors, read reviews and request quotes. Thumbtack suits parties and smaller events, where you pay for leads and need to reply fast. For companies, ezCater lists you for office orders and takes a commission, which the workbook models at {{marketplace_comision}} of the sales that come through it. Add LinkedIn and direct outreach to office managers and planners. Some venues charge an outside vendor fee, so price it into the quote before you accept. Use the directories to win new clients, and invite repeat clients to book directly.
72: Direct selling works if you are willing to go out and meet people. Start with the venues, wedding planners and office managers in your area, and bring a one-page sheet with the menu styles, the packages and a starting price per guest. Ask to be added to a venue's preferred vendor list: a venue that recommends you sends bookings at no advertising cost. Offer a live tasting to the planners who book the most, since someone who has seen you cook recommends you with more confidence. Bridal shows let you meet couples in person. After every visit, send an email and set a reminder. A steady rhythm of small contacts each week works better than one big campaign.
73: The tasting is the step closest to the sale, so budget it as a line in the plan (the P&L carries it as tastings for prospects). Offer it to serious prospects, mainly couples and companies with big events, with a small spread of two or three meats and a printed proposal. You can charge for it and credit it to the contract if the client signs. The proposal lists the menu, the guest count, the staff, the price per guest and the guest minimum. Ask for a 50% deposit to hold the date, nonrefundable as the operators we read do, with the balance due 72 hours before a private party or 14 days before a wedding. Companies usually pay on net 30 terms. Follow up within a day.
74: The best marketing comes after the event. Ask for a Google review within a few days, while the client still remembers the party, and send a short thank-you with a photo if they agree. Companies that reorder get a simple process: their usual menu saved and one named contact. Ask happy clients to introduce you to a friend planning a graduation or a colleague who books lunches, and thank them with a small gesture. Families that book one birthday often return for the next celebration. A referral habit run well costs less than any new lead.
75: The example reserves {{marketing_anual}} a year for marketing, mostly for The Knot and WeddingWire listings, Google Ads, Thumbtack leads, photography and bridal shows, plus the launch budget, which is already in the investment. Record where each lead comes from (website, directory, venue, planner, referral or ezCater) and calculate the marketing cost per event won. If a channel wins events at a lower cost, it gets more budget; if not, drop it. Review the numbers every quarter and adjust.
